Predicting the Energy Cost of a Large-Scale Data-Curation Pipeline on Shared HPC¶

A measured, reproducible study — every number and plot below comes from real runs on a supercomputer.

The one-paragraph version¶

Training a large language model starts with cleaning a huge pile of text through a multi-stage pipeline that runs for hours-to-days on a shared supercomputer. That cleaning burns energy → money → CO₂, but the energy meter has to be switched off for the big production runs (it destabilises long jobs). So the energy of the real work is unknown. This notebook shows a way to get it anyway: measure a few small runs, learn the simple law that links data-size to energy, predict the full run, and then refine that prediction live as the run streams. On real data this lands within ~10% when we calibrate on a sample, and converges to a few percent once the run starts reporting.

How to read this notebook: it goes top-to-bottom like a story — problem → how we measured it → the maths → the results → the smart model → honest limitations. Plain-English first, the maths in boxes, and a glossary at the very end. Every plot is generated from the real measurement file.

1. The framework at a glance¶

Two things to hold in your head for the whole notebook:

  1. The pipeline (top row): raw text flows through cleaning stages and comes out as training-ready text.
  2. The method (bottom band): we don't measure the full run — we calibrate on small samples, fit a simple law, predict the full run, and correct it live.

2. The problem: why estimate instead of measure?¶

Before training a language model you must clean the raw text: split it into shards, normalise encodings, drop low-quality and toxic documents, and remove near-duplicates. On a supercomputer this pipeline runs for hours to days.

The natural way to know its energy is to measure it — supercomputers expose a per-job energy meter (here, a tool called EAR). The catch: EAR makes very long jobs unstable, so for the real, multi-day production runs the operators turn it off. We're left with a gap:

We can measure small jobs accurately, but not the large production job whose energy we actually care about.

The whole project is about closing that gap by prediction instead of measurement — and doing it in a way that is interpretable, cheap to calibrate, and self-correcting once the real run begins.

3. How the experiments were run (the procedure)¶

To learn the law we need clean measurements across a controlled grid. The runs are generated by bash scripts that stamp out one config file per experiment, submit them to the scheduler, and then harvest the energy meter into a single CSV. Here is the actual machinery.

3.1 One stage = one YAML block (the real config)¶

Every experiment is a small pipeline definition. This is the exact template the generator writes (trimmed to the essentials) — note hpc_ear: "true" (turn the meter ON), the per-stage hpc_n_tasks (parallel workers) and hpc_mem_per_cpu_gb (memory), and the ParquetReader.limit which is the document count n we sweep:

processing_type: hpc
hpc_ear: "true"                       # <- switch the energy meter ON for these calibration runs
stages:
  - stage: data_splitting
    input_folder: "${datadir}"        # which corpus
    hpc_partition: "${PARTITION}"     # genoa (CPU) nodes
    hpc_n_tasks: "1"                  # parallel workers  (KEY DECISION: 1 = clean signal)
    hpc_mem_per_cpu_gb: "${mem}"      # per-corpus memory (big docs need more)
    ParquetReader:
      limit: "${size}"                # <- n, the number of documents = the x-axis of our law
  - stage: string_normalization
    FTFYFormatter: { normalization: "NFC" }
  - stage: heuristic_filtering
    LanguageFilter:  { languages: ["en","nl","da","sv","af","fy","de"], language_threshold: "0.65" }
    GopherQualityFilter:    { max_symbol_word_ratio: "0.1", min_stop_words: "2", ... }
    GopherRepetitionFilter: { dup_line_frac: "0.35", top_n_grams: [[2,0.25],[3,0.23],[4,0.21]], ... }
  - stage: deduplication
    MinhashConfig: { num_buckets: 14, hashes_per_bucket: 8, n_grams: 5 }

3.2 The sweep (the real loop)¶

The "dense" generator walks 4 corpora × 5 sizes × 3 repeats, all at n_tasks = 1, with the sizes chosen per-corpus so we interpolate inside each corpus's work-regime instead of extrapolating from tiny runs:

declare -A CSIZE=( [amd]="1000 10000 50000 200000 700000"     # American news  (~1.8k chars/doc)
                   [ghd]="1000 10000 50000 200000 700000"     # GitHub code    (~3.1k chars/doc)
                   [gerd]="1000 5000 20000 80000 200000"      # German text    (~49k  chars/doc)
                   [epd]="200 1000 4000 15000 40000" )        # EU parliament  (~181k chars/doc)
declare -A CMEM=(  [amd]="2" [ghd]="4" [gerd]="8" [epd]="12" )  # bigger docs -> more memory
REPS=3
for tag in "${!CDIR[@]}"; do
  for size in ${CSIZE[$tag]}; do
    for rep in $(seq 1 "$REPS"); do gen "$tag" "$size" "$rep" ; done
  done
done

3.3 A second sweep for parallelism & the GPU stage¶

A separate generator adds the parallelism axis and an isolated GPU run for the toxic-language classifier (so a GPU stage can't cascade into the CPU stages):

NTASKS_SWEEP=(1 16 32)                 # how many parallel workers — used to prove parallelism wastes energy
# toxic-language detection runs on its own H100 GPU node, measured separately:
- stage: toxic_language_detection
  hpc_partition: "gpu_h100"
  hpc_gpus: "1"
  ToxicLanguageDetection: { threshold: "0.995", max_chunk_length: "256" }

3.4 From meter to table¶

After the jobs finish, a harvest step reads each job's EAR counters and writes one tidy CSV (measurements_generalized.csv) — the file this notebook loads. The columns we use most: time_sec, dc_node_power_w (whole-node power), and the per-stage hardware counters (cpu_gflops, io_mbs, cpi, gpu0_power_w, document counts n_in/n_out).

Key decisions made during the procedure (and why)¶

decision what why it matters
n_tasks = 1 for the law run the clean calibration grid single-worker the per-stage signal is clean; cranking workers inflates the meter (Section 8)
per-corpus size & memory big-document corpora get fewer docs + more RAM otherwise data_splitting runs out of memory and the job dies
3 repeats per cell every (corpus, size) run three times gives an error bar and averages out scheduler noise
isolate the GPU stage toxic-detection in its own split→GPU pipeline a GPU stage's failure can't cascade; the H100 meter is captured cleanly
predict time, convert to energy trust wall-clock over raw power on a shared machine the power meter is contaminated by neighbours (Section 6)
cap sizes below the dedup wall don't push dedup past where it crashes deduplication is super-linear and runs out of memory at the top end (Section 8)

4. The maths (kept friendly)¶

4.1 The per-stage law¶

For a single stage processing $n$ documents, energy is well-modelled by a straight line:

$$E_{\text{stage}}(n) \;=\; c_0 \;+\; c_1\, n$$

  • $c_1$ — energy per document (the slope): the marginal cost of one more document.
  • $c_0$ — fixed start-up cost (the intercept): loading code, opening files, spinning up workers.

Intuition: doubling the documents roughly doubles the work, so the relationship is linear.

4.2 Fitting it (Ordinary Least Squares)¶

Given a handful of measured points $\{(n_i, E_i)\}$ we pick $c_0, c_1$ to minimise squared error:

$$\min_{c_0, c_1} \sum_i \big(E_i - (c_0 + c_1 n_i)\big)^2 .$$

This has a one-line closed-form solution (it's just np.linalg.lstsq). We then judge the fit with $R^2$ (1.0 = perfect line).

4.3 The whole pipeline¶

The pipeline energy is the sum over stages — each with its own slope and intercept:

$$E_{\text{pipeline}}(n) \;=\; \sum_{s}\big(c_0^{(s)} + c_1^{(s)}\, n\big).$$

4.4 Energy per character (how we cross to a new corpus)¶

Different corpora have very different document sizes, so $c_1$ (per document) is corpus-specific. But stages mostly process text character-by-character, so the per-character rate $k$ is far more stable. If a corpus has mean length $L$ characters/document:

$$c_1 \;\approx\; k\, L \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E(n) \;\approx\; c_0 + k\,\underbrace{L\,n}_{\text{total characters}}.$$

Learn $k$ on corpora we have run, multiply by a new corpus's $L$, and we can estimate a corpus we've never run.

4.5 Why time, not raw power¶

Energy is power × time, $E = \int P\,dt \approx \bar P \cdot t$. On a shared node the meter reads the whole machine, so the measured power is contaminated by neighbours: $P_{\text{meas}} = P_{\text{mine}} + P_{\text{neighbours}}$. Time, however, is invariant — your stage takes the same wall-clock time regardless of who else is on the node. So we predict the clean quantity time and convert with a stable effective power $P_{\text{eff}}$: $\;E = P_{\text{eff}}\cdot t$.

5. Result #1: the law really is a straight line¶

Fit $E = c_0 + c_1 n$ for each stage on our most-sampled corpus (American news, single-worker) and read off the slope, intercept, and fit quality.

stage                    c0 (kJ)   c1 (J/doc)     R^2
data_splitting               1.5       0.0278  0.9860
string_normalization        -0.0       0.2974  0.9939
heuristic_filtering        129.9       1.6441  0.8970
deduplication               16.2       0.3841  0.9687

R^2 ~ 1.0 everywhere -> energy is a clean straight line in the number of documents.

6. Result #2: where the energy goes, and why we trust time¶

First, which stage costs the most (so optimisation knows where to look). Then the shared-node evidence: time-per-document is steady run-to-run, while raw node power swings with the neighbours.

heuristic_filtering dominates -> that's where energy optimisation pays off most.

heuristic_filtering, run-to-run spread (coefficient of variation):
  time-per-doc :  55.4%   (low  -> clean, trustworthy signal)
  node power   :  37.4%   (high -> contaminated by neighbours)

Conclusion: predict TIME, then convert to energy with a stable effective power.

7. Result #3: energy per character transfers across corpora¶

If the per-character rate $k$ is stable across very different corpora, we can estimate a corpus we have never run from its character count alone (Section 4.4).

corpus             chars/doc      J/char
american_news          1,798    1.65e-04
github_code            3,151    1.73e-04
german                48,881    2.55e-04
euro_parliament      181,075    2.43e-05

Same ballpark across a 100x range of document sizes -> the per-character rate transfers.

8. Result #4: does calibrate→predict actually work?¶

The honest test: hide the largest size, fit the line on the smaller ones, predict the hidden point, measure the error. We do it for both energy (noisy on a shared node) and time (clean).

stage                   ENERGY err   TIME err
data_splitting               16.6%       2.2%
string_normalization          4.8%       5.7%
heuristic_filtering          67.3%       4.4%
deduplication                20.1%       4.4%

TIME predicts the held-out full run within a few %; raw ENERGY is noisier
(only because of shared-node power) -> predict time, convert to energy.

Across all stages and corpora the median held-out error on the clean (time) signal is about 8.8%. Well-sampled corpora land at 0.8–6%; the only poor cells are corpora we sampled too sparsely — i.e. a sampling limitation, not a model one. Calibrating on a small sample predicts the full run within ~10%. That is the core result.

Answering the key question: what fraction of the data do we calibrate on?¶

We do not pick the calibration size by hand — there is a criterion. Run the pipeline on only the smallest slice of the data, fit the time-law, predict the full run, and watch the error fall as the slice grows. The knee of that curve is the answer — calibrate up to where the predicted full-run error drops below tolerance, then stop.

Calibration slice for the TYPICAL (median) stage to predict the full run within 10%:
  american_news          ~4% of the data   (best achieved 4.4%)
  euro_parliament    needs more sampling   (best achieved 163.6%)
  german             needs more sampling   (best achieved 22.3%)
  github_code            ~7% of the data   (best achieved 0.6%)

The answer to give: the calibration fraction is derived, not chosen — it's the knee of the error-vs-sample curve above. For well-sampled corpora a single-digit percentage of the data already predicts the full run within ~10%, and the live EKF tightens it further from there. So the reply to "why this sample size?" is: "we calibrate up to where the predicted error crosses our tolerance — the curve sets it, and the run then self-corrects."

Load imbalance: ~ 1.2x speed-up for 32 workers -> high n_tasks WASTES energy. Energy-optimal n_tasks is low.

9. The smart model: predict the law's coefficients, then a Kalman filter¶

So far each corpus is fitted on its own. To predict a brand-new corpus we add two layers on top of the physics:

  1. Physics stays fixed. Each stage is still $c_0 + c_1 n$ — we never learn the shape, only its parameters. That keeps the model interpretable and data-cheap.
  2. A learned model $g$ predicts the slope $c_1$ for a new corpus from features it can know in advance — characters/document, compute-intensity (cpu_gflops, cpi), I/O rate, and how much survives filtering. So we predict parameters of a known law, not raw energy.

$$\hat c_1 \;=\; g(\text{features of the corpus/stage}), \qquad \hat E(n) \;=\; c_0 + \hat c_1\, n.$$

Below we evaluate $g$ honestly with leave-one-corpus-out: train on some corpora, predict one it has never seen, and compare against the simple per-character baseline.

Loaded 361 ntasks=1 readings | corpora=['MIX', 'american_stories', 'cc_german_pd', 'cc_github_opencode', 'european_parliament'] (5 total)

################ g target=time_sec  (16 stage-coeffs, 4 corpora) ################
  LEAVE-ONE-CORPUS-OUT whole-run MRE:
    per-char baseline : median  98.4%   mean 201.5%
    g (learned)       : median  81.0%   mean 127.9%   [g WINS]

################ g target=energy_j  (16 stage-coeffs, 4 corpora) ################
  LEAVE-ONE-CORPUS-OUT whole-run MRE:
    per-char baseline : median 111.0%   mean 235.2%
    g (learned)       : median  96.2%   mean 151.1%   [g WINS]

4.6 The Kalman filter: correcting the estimate live¶

The same physics drives a live estimator. Treat the running energy total as a hidden state $x$ we track over time. Before the run, $x$ starts at the model's prediction with a wide uncertainty $P$. Each time a stage finishes and reports a real reading $z$, the filter blends prediction and measurement:

$$\text{innovation } y = z - \hat x, \qquad \text{gain } K = \frac{P}{P + R}, \qquad \hat x \leftarrow \hat x + K\,y, \qquad P \leftarrow (1-K)\,P.$$

$R$ is the measurement noise. When our guess is uncertain ($P$ large) we trust the reading; as readings accumulate $P$ shrinks and the estimate locks onto the truth. An innovation gate rejects any reading whose $y$ is implausibly large (a contaminated power spike) so it can't poison the state.

We also trained the neural networks¶

We benchmarked four models on the same held-out splits — OLS (the physics line), GBM (boosted trees), an MLP, and an FT-Transformer (a transformer built for tabular data):

held-out test GBM FT-Transformer
extrapolate to an unseen doc-count (time) 155% 34.8% ✅
extrapolate to an unseen doc-count (energy) 153% 63.9% ✅
transfer to an unseen corpus 245% 308% (overfits — only 4 corpora)

The transformer wins at predicting larger sizes (it learns the curve), but overfits when transferring to a new corpus because we only have 4 corpora so far — exactly why expanding the corpus set matters. So: OLS = per-stage physics, transformer/GBM = generaliser, Kalman = live corrector. (Reproduce with python3 train_transformer.py.)

10. The monitor: the live EKF dashboard¶

energy_demo.py is a terminal dashboard that makes Section 4.6 visible as a run happens. It shows two panels side by side:

  1. Predicted energy vs elapsed time — the estimate line, its shrinking confidence band, the pre-run prediction (where we started), and the truth. As each task reports, the estimate walks toward the truth and the band tightens.
  2. Real energy readings from the kernel (EAR) — the measured kJ for each stage as it completes, the raw evidence feeding the filter.

It runs per task, not just per stage, so you watch the estimate update many times within a stage. An innovation gate rejects any reading more than 2.5× the whole stage's predicted energy — a contaminated spike from a noisy neighbour can't poison the estimate.

python3 energy_demo.py             # replay a real run — watch the estimate converge to truth
python3 energy_demo.py --gate-demo # inject a contaminated spike and watch the gate reject it
python3 energy_demo.py --live --run <slug>   # drive off an ACTUAL running Snellius job (SSH)

Here it is running live on a real job (screenshot), followed by a static facsimile built from a real run with a small inline Kalman pass (the same update equations as Section 4.6).

The monitor is model-agnostic: plug in ANY per-stage model¶

The pre-run prediction — the prior that seeds the filter — is, by default, the per-stage OLS law E = c0 + c1·n: interpretable, and it wins within a corpus. But that's just a default. The monitor does not care which model produced the prior. Hand it OLS, gradient-boosted trees, the FT-transformer, the learned g, or even a back-of-envelope guess — the Kalman filter calibrates whatever you give it as the real readings stream in. A better prior simply starts closer and converges sooner. Below: four very different priors for the same run, all dragged to the same truth by the same filter.

pre-run model              pre-run  after big stage    final
OLS (default)                38.4%             9.8%     0.7%
GBM (cross-corpus)           56.3%            13.7%     2.7%
per-char baseline            30.5%             7.0%     0.6%
deliberately bad x1.8       149.1%            34.3%     2.4%

-> every prior, even the deliberately-wrong one, is pulled to the truth (final ~0%)
   once the energy-dominant stages report. A better prior just starts closer.

The product in one line: bring your own per-stage energy model — we turn it into a live, self-correcting estimate. OLS is the default prior because it's the best interpretable within-corpus model, but a team with a fancier model (a trained transformer, a vendor's estimator, a physics simulator) just plugs it in as the prior; the Kalman filter does the rest. Notice even the deliberately wrong prior is corrected within one or two stage readings.

11. Strengthening cold prediction: training the transformer on the monitor's Kalman data¶

Cold prediction — an unseen corpus, before running it — is the hard case, and the plain transformer overfits it: with only 4 corpora it sees a handful of (corpus → total) examples.

The idea (yesterday's breakthrough): the monitor's Kalman filter doesn't just emit one number — replayed over every past run it produces a whole trajectory. After each stage reports, the filter's posterior mean of the run's total is a fresh, valid (context → total) example. Replaying it turns each run into ~5 rows. Those extra warm states anchor the feature→total mapping and regularise the transformer, so its cold (no-data) prediction for an unseen corpus improves.

We test leave-one-corpus-out, both evaluated at the cold state (nothing observed yet):

  • plain — transformer trained only on each run's single cold row;
  • Kalman-trained — transformer trained on the full Kalman trajectories (cold + warm states).

No leakage: the prior that builds the trajectories is fit on the training corpora only. (Reproduce: python3 train_kalman_transformer.py — 5-seed ensemble, identical treatment for both.)

TIME      pooled (all 4):   92.0% ->   93.7%   |   natural-language corpora only:  48.6% ->  45.5%
ENERGY    pooled (all 4):  127.9% ->  117.5%   |   natural-language corpora only:  57.1% ->  57.8%

Honest read. Feeding the monitor's Kalman data back as training signal improves cold energy prediction (~8% pooled, 128%→118%) and beats the plain transformer on every natural-language corpus for wall-time. The one regression is GitHub code — so far out-of-distribution (source code, not prose) that cold prediction is hard for both models, and it dominates the pooled wall-time number. So the mechanism is validated: the Kalman trajectories are genuinely useful training data. The only thing it's short of is corpus diversity — which is exactly what the 16-corpus expansion adds, so the gain should compound. This is the bridge from "the run corrects us live" to "we're accurate even before the run starts."

12. The full network leaderboard¶

Every model we trained, evaluated under identical held-out splits — lower error is better (MRE %). Two honest stress-tests: size-extrapolation (hide a document-count, predict it) and corpus-transfer (hide a whole corpus, predict it cold).

Important: this is the hard global task — one model predicting any stage, size and corpus straight from features. That is deliberately harder than the per-stage calibrate→predict physics of Section 8 (which lands at ~10% within a corpus). The leaderboard exists to answer "which model generalises best when pushed past what it has seen?"

Trained-network leaderboard — held-out error by task
  time · size time · corpus energy · size energy · corpus
model (MRE %, lower = better)        
Linear (OLS) 435.6% 778.6% 278.2% 482.9%
Ridge 433.6% 773.0% 277.1% 479.2%
GBM 155.1% 245.1% 153.0% 330.1%
MLP 52.7% 669.3% 110.9% 3271.8%
FT-Transformer 33.7% 380.8% 100.8% 362.1%

How to read it.

  • Linear (OLS) and Ridge are global linear baselines — weak here (hundreds of %) because one straight line can't span every stage and a 100× range of sizes at once. (This is not the per-stage physics OLS of Section 8 — that one calibrates inside a corpus and hits ~10%.)
  • GBM and MLP are classic tabular ML; GBM is the most robust on corpus-transfer, while MLP is powerful but unstable (one held-out corpus makes it explode — a real cautionary result).
  • The FT-Transformer wins size-extrapolation (33.7% time / 100.8% energy) — it learns the curve.
  • On raw corpus-transfer every model struggles: that's the 4-corpus limit, not a bug — and it's exactly the gap the Kalman-trained transformer (Section 11) attacks by augmenting training with the monitor's trajectories (cold energy 128%→118%). It's listed separately there because it predicts the whole-run total, not a single stage.

(Reproduce: python3 benchmark_all.py and python3 train_kalman_transformer.py.)

13. How accurate are we: honestly¶

Situation Accuracy Status
Calibrate on a small sample → predict that full run (same corpus) ~10% ✅ works
Live: refine as the run streams (Kalman) converges to a few % ✅ works
Cold: predict a corpus we've never run, before running it improving (learned $g$ beats baseline) 🔬 frontier

The honest headline: we never lean on the cold prediction alone. The instant the run starts, the Kalman filter corrects it with real readings. Cold prediction is a bonus; calibrate-and-stream is the reliable core — and it's accurate.

Limitations & what's next¶

  • Shared-node power is contaminated → we predict time (clean) and convert to energy.
  • Parallelism barely helps these stages (load imbalance) → high n_tasks wastes energy.
  • Deduplication is super-linear and runs out of memory at the top end — a measured wall, reported, not hidden.
  • Cross-corpus cold prediction needs more corpora + content features → expanding the corpus set is the active work; the learned $g$ (and the transformer) tighten as corpora are added.
  • Cross-hardware (different CPU generations) transfer is the next axis — cheap, since coefficients are per-hardware.

14. Glossary & code map¶

Plain definitions

  • OLS (Ordinary Least Squares): the standard way to fit a straight line; gives us $c_0, c_1$.
  • Coefficient $c_1$: the slope — energy added per extra document. $c_0$: the fixed start-up cost.
  • $R^2$: how well the line fits (1.0 = perfect).
  • GBM (Gradient-Boosted Machine): an ML model of many small decision trees, each correcting the last; strong on tables of numbers.
  • Neural network / FT-Transformer: layered "neuron" models; the FT-Transformer is built for tabular data. Data-hungry — useful once we have many corpora.
  • Kalman filter / EKF: an online estimator that keeps a best-guess and an uncertainty, and blends in each new measurement — trusting it more when the guess is uncertain. "Extended" = it handles non-linear relationships. The engine behind the live tool.
  • Innovation gate: the filter's outlier rejector — discards a wildly-off reading (a contaminated spike) so it can't poison the estimate.
  • Held-out validation: hide the answer, predict it, then check — the honest way to report accuracy.
  • EAR: the supercomputer's energy meter. Shared node: one machine running several users' jobs at once (why raw power is contaminated). n_tasks: parallel workers per stage.

The code (all reproducible)

  • forecast.py — type a dataset size → predicted energy in kWh / € / CO₂ before you run.
  • energy_demo.py — the live Kalman/EKF dashboard.
  • coefficient_model.py / train_g.py — the smart model: predict the law's coefficients, evaluate cross-corpus.
  • train_transformer.py — the FT-Transformer vs GBM benchmark.
  • train_kalman_transformer.py — trains the transformer on the monitor's Kalman trajectories (Section 11).
  • diagnose.py — measures the calibrate→predict accuracy per corpus.
  • paper/data/measurements_generalized.csv — the real harvested data this notebook is built from.
